files.lesson.md: --- order: 5 unit: statistics node: [AC9M7ST02 n2, AC9M7ST02 n3] title: Comparing data sets summary: "Describe a data set by its shape (symmetrical or skewed, with clusters, gaps or outliers), its centre and its spread. Compare two sets on centre and spread, with numbers and in context, not by one value." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Two classes sit the same quiz. One has the top score; the other has nobody below 12. Which class did better? It depends on what you compare." connection: bus-lateness # data/connections/maths.yml (pilot: Make on paper and Also used in; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8183 url: http://127.0.0.1:8183/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: data.yml#explain, caption: "Class B's median (16) is a little higher, but its range (16) is much wider than Class A's (6): A is more consistent." } explainClip: query: { code: "@data.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Compare centre and spread" say: "Compare two data sets on their centre and their spread." clip: - caption: { text: "Centre: the medians are 15 (A) and 16 (B). Close.", say: "Centre: the medians are fifteen and sixteen. Close." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "Spread: the ranges are 6 (A) and 16 (B). A is much more consistent.", say: "Spread: the ranges are six and sixteen. Class A is much more consistent." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "A good comparison names both, with numbers and in context.", say: "A good comparison names both, with numbers, in context." } - wait: 1400 --- To describe a data set, look at three things: - **Shape**: is it **symmetrical** (balanced about the middle) or **skewed** (bunched at one end with a tail at the other)? Are there **clusters**, **gaps** or **outliers**? - **Centre**: the median (or mean): a typical value. - **Spread**: the range: how varied the values are. To **compare** two data sets, compare their centres **and** their spreads, using the numbers and saying what they mean in context. ## Predict: more consistent ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to which class is more consistent before the board shows the ranges separates centre from spread." check: type: predict q: "Quiz scores. Class A: $12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18$. Class B: $6, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22$. Which class's scores are more consistent?" options: - "Class A" - "Class B" - "They are the same" actual: "Class A. Its scores range from 12 to 18 (a range of 6); Class B's go from 6 to 22 (a range of 16). The centres are close: medians 15 and 16." ``` Look at how far apart each class's lowest and highest scores are. ## Run: change the centre ```step stage: run insight: "Changing one class's scores and watching both medians and ranges shows that centre and spread are separate: one can change without the other." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Change Class A's scores (click or type) so that Class A's median is higher than Class B's. Was your prediction right about consistency?", when: "d > D" } ``` Did the range change when the median moved? Can you raise the median without changing the range? ## Investigate: describe, then compare ```step stage: investigate insight: "Shape, centre and spread describe one set; comparing two needs both centre and spread, with numbers and context. Mia's mistake compares the single highest values." tasks: - picture: { ref: data.yml#skewed, caption: "Number of books read this term by a class." } check: type: question q: "Which describes the shape of this data?" options: ["Skewed: most values are low, with a tail of a few high values", "Symmetrical about the middle", "Every value is equally common"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Most dots are bunched at the low end, with a few far to the right.", "Count the dots: 2 is much more common than 9."] explain: "Most students read 1 to 3 books, a few read many: the data is skewed, with a tail to the right." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mia" text: "Mia compares the two classes. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: compare-single-value explain: "Line 3: one student's score does not describe a class. Compare centres (medians 15 and 16: close) and spreads (ranges 6 and 16: A is much more consistent)." - check: type: question q: "Which is the best comparison of Class A and Class B?" options: ["The classes have similar medians (15 and 16), but Class A's scores are much less spread (range 6 against 16), so A was more consistent.", "Class B is better because it has a 22.", "Class A is better because 15 + 14 is more than 6 + 10."] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "One score is not the class.", "That compares a few values, not the whole data."] explain: "A good comparison names the centre and the spread of both, with numbers, and says what they mean." ``` ### Shape, centre, spread Here is how to describe and compare. ```worked \text{Shape} :: Symmetrical, or skewed with a tail? Clusters, gaps, outliers? \text{Centre: medians } 15 \text{ and } 16 :: Close: a typical score is about the same. \text{Spread: ranges } 6 \text{ and } 16 :: Very different: Class B's scores vary much more. \text{Compare both} :: "Similar centres, but A is more consistent (range 6, not 16)." ``` Now describe the shape of the books data. ### Find the mistake Read Mia's reasoning. What does one score tell you about a class? ### A good comparison ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: same centre with a different spread on the board, a symmetrical shape, an outlier, a difference in medians, then the edge case of equal means hiding different spreads." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#same-median", height: 640 } tasks: - starter: "data.yml#same-median" hint: ["Team A's median is the middle value, 10: keep it.", "Bring the lowest and highest values closer to 10."] check: { type: board, text: "Change Team A so its median stays 10 but its range is smaller than Team B's.", when: "d = 10 and r < R and n = 5", explain: "For example 8, 9, 10, 11, 12: median 10, range 4, less than B's 7." } - picture: { ref: data.yml#symmetric, caption: "Hours of sleep on a school night." } check: type: question q: "Describe the shape." options: ["Roughly symmetrical, centred about 6", "Skewed to the right", "Two separate clusters"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The dots rise to a peak at 6 and fall away evenly on both sides.", "There is no gap: it is one group."] explain: "The data is balanced about 6 hours: symmetrical." - check: type: question q: "Times (s): $13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 29$. Which value is an outlier?" options: ["29", "13", "There is none"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "13 is next to the others.", "29 is far from the rest."] explain: "29 is far from the cluster of 13 to 16." - check: type: answer q: "Class A's median is 15 and Class B's is 16. By how much is B's median higher?" answer: "1" feedback: - ["31", "Find the difference, not the total."] explain: "16 − 15 = 1: a small difference in typical scores." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: two sets have the same mean, 10: Set P is $9, 10, 11$ and Set Q is $0, 10, 20$. Are they alike?" options: ["No: same centre, but Q is much more spread (range 20 against 2)", "Yes: same mean, same data"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Look at the spread: 2 against 20."] explain: "A centre alone hides the spread: always compare both." ``` ### Same centre, smaller spread Each task changes one thing. ### Symmetrical ### An outlier ### Difference in centre ### Same mean ## Practise: compare in context ```step stage: practise insight: "Describing shape and comparing centres and spreads in new contexts, mixed; the single-value slip planted again; the review keeps stem-and-leaf reading fresh." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Two bakeries' delivery times (min). Bakery X: median 25, range 10. Bakery Y: median 22, range 30. Which statement is right?" options: ["Y is usually a bit faster, but X is more reliable", "X is faster and more reliable", "Y is slower and more reliable"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "X's median (25) is higher: slower on a typical day.", "Y's median (22) is lower: faster on a typical day."] explain: "Lower median: Y is faster typically. Smaller range: X is more reliable." - check: type: question q: "Which is NOT a fair comparison of two netball teams' goals?" options: ["Team 1 scored the single highest game, so Team 1 is better", "Team 1's median was 3 goals higher", "Team 2's goals varied less (smaller range)"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is fair: it compares centres.", "That is fair: it compares spreads."] explain: "One game does not describe a team." - check: type: question q: "Data bunched at the high end with a few low values. What shape is it?" options: ["Skewed, with a tail to the left", "Skewed, with a tail to the right", "Symmetrical"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The tail is where the few values are: the low end, on the left.", "Most values are at one end."] explain: "The tail points towards the few low values: to the left." - check: type: answer q: "Review: a stem-and-leaf plot reads $2 \\mid 1\\ 4\\ 6$ and $3 \\mid 0\\ 5$. What is the median?" answer: "26" feedback: - ["6", "Read the whole value: 2 | 6 is 26."] explain: "Values 21, 24, 26, 30, 35: the 3rd is 26." ``` ### Centre and spread ### A fair comparison ### Skewed ### Review: stem-and-leaf ## Make: a surprising comparison ```step stage: make insight: "Making one set have the higher median but the lower mean shows that the measures can disagree, so a comparison should say which it uses." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#make", height: 640 } hint: ["Set B's median is 15 and its mean 15.6.", "Give Set A a middle value above 15, but some very low values to drag its mean down."] check: { type: board, text: "Change Set A (5 values) so it has a higher median than Set B but a lower mean.", when: "n = 5 and d > D and m < M", explain: "For example 1, 2, 16, 17, 18: median 16 (more than 15), mean 10.8 (less than 15.6)." } ``` Write two headlines about your sets: one where A wins, one where B wins. ## Make: two bus routes on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Comparing two bus routes needs a centre and a spread for each; the paper task makes them compute both and choose the reason that uses both." hint: ["Write each list in order first.", "Median: the 4th of 7 values."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Two bus routes get you to school. Over 7 school days, Route 52 was 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5 and 20 minutes late. Route 7 was 2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6 and 6 minutes late. How many minutes later is Route 7's median than Route 52's? Then say which route is more reliable." steps: - ["Route 52: median 3 min, range $20 - 1 = 19$ min", "the median is the 4th of 7 values"] - ["Route 7: median 5 min, range $6 - 2 = 4$ min", "same steps for the other route"] - ["$5 - 3 = 2$ min", "Route 7's median is 2 min later"] - ["Route 7 is more reliable: it is usually 2 min later, but never more than 6 min late, while Route 52 was once 20 min late", "use a centre and a spread, in context"] picks: - step: 4 q: "Which sentence compares the routes well?" options: - "Route 7 is later in the middle, but its spread is small; Route 52 is usually earlier but swings a lot" - "Route 52 is better: its median is lower" - "Route 52 is better: its earliest day was 1 min late" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That uses the centre only. The 20-minute day matters if you must be on time.", "That is one value from one set. Compare a centre and a spread for both."] answer: "2" feedback: - ["19", "That is Route 52's range. Take the two medians away from each other."] - ["5", "That is Route 7's median. How much later is it than Route 52's?"] criteria: - "I found a median and a range for both routes." - "My comparison uses a centre and a spread, with the bus times in it." - "I did not judge by one value from each set." explain: "Medians 3 and 5, so Route 7's is 2 min later. Ranges 19 and 4: Route 7 is steadier. If you must be at school on time, Route 7 is the safer bus." ``` Do this one in your book. The lateness figures are made up, but a real class could log them in a week. Work out both medians and both ranges on paper, type the difference in medians, then choose the sentence that compares the routes well. **Also used in** - **Choosing a route.** Which bus is more reliable is a centre-and-spread question, and a week or two of recording answers it better than a guess. - **Classes and brands.** Which class did better, or which battery lasts longer, needs the same two numbers for each set. - **Waiting times.** Queues and waits are usually skewed: most are short and a few are very long, so the spread tells you more than the average. ```teacher summary: Students describe data sets by shape (symmetrical or skewed, clusters, gaps, outliers), centre and spread, and compare two sets on both centre and spread, with numbers and in context (AC9M7ST02, nodes 2 and 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 13 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can describe the shape of a data set (symmetrical, skewed, clusters, gaps, outliers). - I can compare two data sets using a measure of centre and a measure of spread. - I can write a comparison with numbers and in context. struggle: "Using a centre and a spread together, in words. Ask: which route is later in the middle, and which is steadier?" before: > Do the Run and Make boards first. Students need Mean, median, mode and range, and Stem-and-leaf plots. The one idea: a data set has a shape, a centre and a spread; comparing two needs both centre and spread. The common mistake is comparing single values (the highest score); it is planted in Mia's reasoning and again in Practise. The board draws the second set above the first, each with its own median line and range arrow; only the first set can be changed. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands; ask students who chose B why (often the 22)." - "Run: ask whether raising the median changed the range." - "Investigate: write a sentence frame on the board: 'On average … (median …), but … is more spread (range …).'" - "Modify: for the same-mean edge case, ask students to invent a third set with mean 10 and range 100." - "Make: read out pairs of headlines." - "Paper: the two bus routes are worked in books (medians and ranges); the page marks the difference in medians and the comparing sentence. Books out, then ask who chose the bus they would catch and why." stuck: - see: A student compares one value from each set (Mia's mistake). ask: Does one student's score describe the whole class? fix: Compare a centre (median) and a spread (range) for each. - see: A student gives numbers without meaning. ask: What does a bigger range mean for these students? fix: "Say it in context: 'less consistent', 'more varied'." - see: A student confuses the direction of skew. ask: Where are the few values that trail off? fix: The tail points to the few values; that is the direction of the skew. stretch: Find two data sets with the same median and range but clearly different shapes. support: Use the sentence frame and the board's measures for every comparison. leads: > Next: the Chance unit (sample spaces and probability). A statistical investigation (AC9M7ST03) is a class task: pose a question, collect data, display and compare it with these tools (see the unit primer). Where it leads: sampling and variation (Year 8), the five-number summary and box plots (Years 9 and 10). exit: q: "Group 1 reaction times (s): median 0.32, range 0.10. Group 2: median 0.28, range 0.35. Compare the groups in one sentence." a: Group 2 was faster on a typical try (median 0.28 s against 0.32 s), but much less consistent (range 0.35 s against 0.10 s). explain: > Describe a data set by its **shape** (symmetrical, or **skewed** with a tail; clusters, gaps, outliers), its **centre** (median or mean) and its **spread** (range). To **compare** two sets, compare the centres **and** the spreads, with numbers and in context: "Similar medians (15 and 16), but Class A is more consistent (range 6 against 16)." One value, such as the highest score, does not describe a set. ```

# Data boards for "Comparing data sets". second: draws a second data set above the first, with its own measures.

# region: run
widget: data
values: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18
second: 6, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22
names: Class A, Class B
range: 0, 25
edit: on
show: mean, median, range
label: Quiz score out of 25
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: data
values: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18
second: 6, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22
names: Class A, Class B
range: 0, 25
show: median, range
label: Quiz score out of 25
# endregion

# region: skewed
widget: data
values: 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9
range: 0, 10
show: none
label: Number of books read this term
# endregion

# region: symmetric
widget: data
values: 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9
range: 0, 12
show: none
label: Hours of sleep on a school night
# endregion

# region: same-median
widget: data
values: 2, 9, 10, 12, 18
second: 6, 8, 10, 11, 13
names: Team A, Team B
range: 0, 20
edit: on
show: median, range
# endregion

# region: make
widget: data
values: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18
second: 5, 13, 15, 15, 30
names: Set A, Set B
range: 0, 35
edit: on
show: mean, median
# endregion

# region: mia
Class A: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18. Class B: 6, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22.
The best score in Class B is 22; in Class A it is 18.
So Class B did better.
